statement: In randomized trials of people with multiple sclerosis (11 trials, 2,138 participants; 3 further trials in paraplegia, 142 participants, could not be pooled; of all 14 trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, most often nabiximols (6 of the 14 trials and 4 of the 5 in the Ashworth pool), in trials whose follow-up, where printed, was 3 to 15 weeks, are associated with a small improvement in spasticity as patients rate it, but not detectably as clinicians measure it. In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), patients' own spasticity ratings (numerical rating or visual analogue scales) were 0.76 points lower (95% CI 0.14 to 1.38 lower; 3 trials, 698 people; I2 73%; low certainty by the review team) and more patients rated themselves improved overall (OR 1.44, 1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 people; low), while the Ashworth scale, a clinician's rating of muscle tone, did not clearly change (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials; I2 0%; moderate; the overall value as corrected by the journal in 2015), nor did the share of people whose rated spasticity fell by at least 30% (OR 1.64, 0.95 to 2.83) or 50% (1.40, 0.81 to 2.41; 2 trials each), activities of daily living (Barthel index: the review prints three separate product estimates and no pooled one, all with intervals that include no difference) or walking speed (-0.86, -3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials). The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for spasticity, but none of the outcomes it rated moderate (Ashworth, Barthel index, walking speed) showed a clear difference. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with MS who took a cannabis medicine, most often a THC and CBD mouth spray, rated their muscle stiffness a little lower (0.76 points on the rating scales used) than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo), and more of them felt better overall. When doctors measured stiffness, there was no clear difference. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
population: People with multiple sclerosis in randomized trials published up to April 2015 (pooled analyses); trials in paraplegia from spinal cord injury not pooled
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials, most often nabiximols (also THC/CBD capsules, dronabinol and nabilone); doses are study conditions
outcome: Spasticity on the Ashworth scale (clinician-rated) and on patient-rated numerical rating or visual analogue scales; 30% and 50% reductions; patients' global impression of change; activities of daily living (Barthel index); walking speed
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, multiple sclerosis trials, random effects, against placebo: patient-rated spasticity (numerical rating or visual analogue scales) WMD -0.76 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.14; 3 trials, 698 patients; I2 73%; GRADE low by the review team); global impression of change OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 patients; low); Ashworth WMD -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials; I2 0%; moderate; the overall as corrected in the abstract in July 2015, also printed in the text and Figure 3; Table 2 gives 1,244 patients, Figure 3's totals 590 and 544; Table 2's three values for this row are per-product estimates, nabiximols -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02, from 4 trials); 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83) and 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41), 2 trials each (low); Barthel index: three estimates printed beside nabilone (2 trials), dronabinol and THC/CBD, -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 0.23 (-0.13 to 0.59) and -0.03 (-0.39 to 0.33), no pooled estimate (moderate); walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials; moderate).

risk_of_bias.note: Of the 14 spasticity trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias; withdrawals and blinding as for the review overall, and patient-rated scales are open to unblinding by psychoactive effects (card sc_whiting_2015).

inconsistency.note: I2 73% for the patient-rated scale (3 trials).

indirectness.note: Worded for short trials of mostly nabiximols in multiple sclerosis.

imprecision.note: The patient-rated difference excludes no effect (698 people) and the Ashworth interval is narrow; the responder analyses, 2 trials each, are imprecise but secondary; the Barthel index has no pooled estimate.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias and one for inconsistency: low, the review team's own rating for the patient-rated outcome. The clinician-rated null (Ashworth, moderate by the review team) fits a small effect that patients notice and the clinicians' scale misses, or patient ratings swayed by knowing the treatment; the trials cannot separate these. Status replicated: the review says studies generally suggested improvement, and the patient-rated and global-impression pools (3 trials each) point the same way; in the Ashworth forest plot (Figure 3, viewed at adjudication) the trial estimates lie on both sides of zero, none significant, and one three-arm trial (Zajicek 2003) enters twice against the same placebo group, with negligible weight.
